newsitem.title: UK: Options -Trade on alert as LME copper expiry looms.
newsitem.headline: Options -Trade on alert as LME copper expiry looms.

text.p: Option traders on the London Metal Exchange (LME) were on full alert this week ahead of what some feared could be an explosive December declaration on Wednesday.
The sharp rally in underlying prices during the second half of November has uncovered some hefty short upside call exposure and subsequent delta hedge buying of futures.
The main concern for some players is if December copper rises towards $2,600 a tonne by the declaration.
"This market could get extremely ugly," a trader said.
"Next week is a cause for nervousness as open interest on that strike alone ($2,600) is twice the size of total stocks."
As at the close of business on Wednesday open interest on LME options at $2,600 was 6,750 lots, equivalent to 168,750 tonnes. LME copper stocks on Friday totalled just 92,475 tonnes.
"The main concern is if this market takes off again. Cash copper at $2,800 is a possibility next week," a second options trader said.
Some of this week's action on futures and options was seen as covering against upside exposure.

Some dealers said an influential short position holder in options appeared to have been squeezed in recent weeks, finally forced to cover call exposure after having defended the upside successfully for several months.
Active buying of $2,500 December calls at up to 50 percent volatility this week may have been part of this, they added.
"I think they have covered some of their needs. But the selling of futures in the last two days may well be them keeping prices down," a third trader said.
"The big shorts are much weaker now," said another. "This time it appears they have got clobbered."
Other options dealers played down the theory that one dominant short had been caught out.
"I find it hard to believe that these people would just sit there with a large options position and not do anything about it. It would be bad risk management," a dealer said.
These traders were less worried about December declarations.
"You will get some volatility over the next few days, but I think people have now tidied a lot of things up," said one.
He added that falling prices since Thursday morning had taken some of the pressure off the options declaration.
December copper peaked at around $2,500 on Thursday. By midday on Friday it was back below $2,400.
Elsewhere in copper some traders saw renewed interest from major copper producers to use higher prices to get some protection on board in 1997 and 1998.
But rather than buying outright downside puts, which are still expensive, some are trading min-max strategies, funding out-of-the-money puts by selling out-of-the-money calls.
"Puts are just too expensive," said one dealer. "Producers accepted they will have to be more proactive and imaginative."
Some producers are also using higher prices to sell forward on the futures market, another options dealer said.
In other metals traders saw a large tranche of aluminium business go through on Thursday involving selling of puts for the first half of 1997 then call selling for the same period.
Several dealers said this was part of a strangle play by a major Korean trade player, although some of the business may have been of a speculative nature.
They saw puts sold at strikes between $1,475 and $1,525 and calls sold between $1,600 and $1,700.
Business was done at around 19 percent volatility and was easily absorbed by a market short of forward aluminium options.
Market makers said the activity appeared to be to raise premiums, but added it also made sense given the seller's physical positions.
Lead volatilities rose this week, driven higher by speculative call buying at $725 and $750.
Zinc attracted light granting of nearby options, but underlying interest in forward upside buying was also evident.
